title: Polyphasic Sleep
author: InsolentCoolRadio
selftext:
Half awake. I’m setting a timer and sleeping for 20 minutes to get up and see if Space Grok (Grok via Cursor) needs anything as it’s working on my Unity animations. Then I’m going back to sleep. I’ll probably repeat this cycle for a few hours.

To what extent is your sleep schedule dependent on AI rate limits and/or agentic coding sprints?

I read in ‘Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution’ that back in the day (like when they had punch cards)programmers used to “phase shift” their sleep cycles because they were awake for a long time every day, which led to a cultural environment where it was normal for people to have bespoke sleep cycles.

I’m wondering to what extent history is rhyming.

Life is a brutal and cruel roguelike. Pick the least horrible option 🧮🤖🏭🤖🫩🤖🏗️🤖👾

comments.body: Dude, use some of those tokens to add guardrails and procedures for when you're away so you can sleep and the agents can keep on trucking. My sleep schedule is the very last thing I'd consider modifying for productivity reasons.

replies.author: InsolentCoolRadio
replies.body:
It's not ideal and I've actually slowed down a bit after the feedback I've been getting from my swarm and other humans.



Outside of things that are mostly novel to the user ("I don't know how to make a game sprite. Make and animate a forest background in Unity where all the trees and animals have their own animation and output a postmortem when you're done.") or things the user has mapped out in detail ("Follow this SOP and make 10 variants of a level using model F2.1, but do NOT include the depressive dragon."), most operations have necessary human gates that are somewhat unpredictable.



For things outside of those gates it's a lot more difficult or even unwise to fully automate without a huge degree of oversight and feedback. But, to your point that oversight and feedback is higher quality when well rested.

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body:
For those you can still generally handle it automatically to a degree even if they can't resolve the thing themselves. Like for my setup if it's a cheap to reverse decision then I let the agent make it and keep a log of their decisions so they can inform me later when I get back. If it's something they can't decide they can escalate to a more powerful model or queue up the questions in that log for when I return. Likewise, nothing goes into `master` without my explicit approval. They're free to make branches, PRs, and stack PRs, but I still have to review and approve the changes and merge it.

With enough work queued up they can generally run without me in the loop for around a day, and longer horizons are definitely possible with the right tooling to support them. I get plenty of sleep and even have open ended gaming time again which is something I had to skip when I was doing all the work myself in the past.
